claim: Acetylcholine enhances cortical sensory responses and perceptual sensitivity in aroused or attentive states.
source: Acetylcholine is well-understood to enhance cortical sensory responses and perceptual sensitivity in aroused or attentive states.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Dialyzing carbachol into HVC increased the pitch of song.
source: We found that dialyzing the cholinergic agonist carbachol into HVC increased the pitch, amplitude, tempo and stereotypy of song, similar to the natural invigoration of song that occurs when males direct their songs to females.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mean ± s.e.m. increase in pitch for Carb: 1.2 ± 0.21%, p=0.00088 vs saline (Figure 1D).

claim: Dialyzing carbachol into HVC increased the amplitude of song.
source: We found that dialyzing the cholinergic agonist carbachol into HVC increased the pitch, amplitude, tempo and stereotypy of song, similar to the natural invigoration of song that occurs when males direct their songs to females.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mean ± s.e.m. increase in amplitude for Carb: 8.3 ± 2.5%, p=0.012 vs saline (Figure 1I).

claim: Dialyzing carbachol into HVC increased the tempo of song.
source: We found that dialyzing the cholinergic agonist carbachol into HVC increased the pitch, amplitude, tempo and stereotypy of song, similar to the natural invigoration of song that occurs when males direct their songs to females.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mean ± s.e.m. reduction in sequence duration for Carb: 2.8 ± 0.43%, p=0.00024 vs saline (Figure 1G).

claim: Dialyzing carbachol into HVC increased the stereotypy of song.
source: We found that dialyzing the cholinergic agonist carbachol into HVC increased the pitch, amplitude, tempo and stereotypy of song, similar to the natural invigoration of song that occurs when males direct their songs to females.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mean ± s.e.m. reduction in pitch c.v. for Carb: 13 ± 1.6%, p=0.0014 vs saline (Figure 1E).

claim: Carbachol-induced effects on song were associated with increased neural activity in HVC.
source: These carbachol-induced effects were associated with increased neural activity in HVC and occurred independently of basal ganglia circuitry.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increase in firing rate in 100 ms window centered on syllable onsets: 9.9 ± 1.4%, p=2.8e-9 (Figure 4D).

claim: Carbachol-induced effects on song occurred independently of basal ganglia circuitry.
source: These carbachol-induced effects were associated with increased neural activity in HVC and occurred independently of basal ganglia circuitry.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that carbachol effects persisted during LMAN inactivation (Figure 3).

claim: The normal invigoration of female-directed song was accompanied by increased HVC activity.
source: Moreover, we discovered that the normal invigoration of female-directed song was also accompanied by increased HVC activity and was attenuated by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increase in firing rate in 100 ms window centered on syllable onsets during directed song: 7.2 ± 1.0%, p=1.1e-15 (Figure 5).

claim: The normal invigoration of female-directed song was attenuated by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: Moreover, we discovered that the normal invigoration of female-directed song was also accompanied by increased HVC activity and was attenuated by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing atropine attenuated social modulation of pitch (p=0.046) and pitch c.v. (p=0.0028) (Figure 6).

claim: Acetylcholine can act directly on cortical premotor circuitry to adaptively shape behavior.
source: These results indicate that, analogous to its influence on sensory systems, acetylcholine can act directly on cortical premotor circuitry to adaptively shape behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing carbachol effects on HVC and song that persist without basal ganglia.

claim: Active and aroused behavioral states are associated with enhanced perceptual capabilities that can aid detection and processing of threats or other salient stimuli.
source: In the sensory domain, active and aroused behavioral states are associated with enhanced perceptual capabilities that can aid detection and processing of threats or other salient stimuli (Bennett et al., 2013; McGinley et al., 2015; Woods et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Greater arousal can enable more rapid, forceful, and precise movements.
source: Analogously, in the motor domain, greater arousal can enable more rapid, forceful, and precise movements—that is, greater vigor—which work in tandem with enhanced sensory processing to coordinate adaptive behavioral responses (Bouman et al., 2015; DiGirolamo et al., 2016; Lovett-Barron et al., 2017; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Acetylcholine has been linked to arousal-related enhancement of sensory processing by direct action on sensory cortices.
source: Acetylcholine, which figures prominently in the ascending arousal system, has been linked to the arousal-related enhancement of sensory processing by direct action on sensory cortices (Fu et al., 2014; Herrero et al., 2008; St Peters et al., 2011; Pinto et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Motor cortical regions receive dense cholinergic innervation from the nucleus basalis.
source: However, while motor cortical regions receive dense cholinergic innervation from the nucleus basalis (NBM; Eckenstein et al., 1988; McKinney et al., 1983; Raghanti et al., 2008), the extent to which cholinergic signaling in cortex contributes to motor invigoration observed in aroused behavioral states remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dopaminergic signaling in the basal ganglia is important for invigorating movements in order to obtain reward and in other motivational contexts.
source: Previous work on the control of movement vigor has focused primarily on dopaminergic signaling in the basal ganglia, which appears to be particularly important for invigorating movements in order to obtain reward and in other motivational contexts (Berke, 2018; Dudman and Krakauer, 2016; Turner and Desmurget, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lesions of NBM and diseases of the cholinergic system can be accompanied by a reduction in the speed, force, and amplitude of movements.
source: Indeed, lesions of NBM and diseases of the cholinergic system can be accompanied by a reduction in the speed, force, and amplitude of movements (Berger-Sweeney et al., 1994; Buchman et al., 2007; Ferris and Farlow, 2013; Goldman et al., 1999), in addition to more general impairments in motor skill acquisition and motor recovery following cortical lesions (Conner et al., 2003; Conner et al., 2005; Conner et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stimulation of NBM can invigorate movements of rat vibrissae that are induced by stimulation of motor cortex.
source: Moreover, stimulation of NBM can invigorate movements of rat vibrissae that are induced by stimulation of motor cortex (Berg et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Female-directed song during courtship is associated with greater pitch and tempo compared to undirected song.
source: In particular, female-directed song during courtship is associated with greater pitch and tempo, altered song amplitude, and increased acoustic stereotypy compared to the undirected song that male birds sing in isolation (Cooper and Goller, 2006; James and Sakata, 2015; Kao et al., 2005; Sakata et al., 2008; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980; Suri and Rajan, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Female-directed song during courtship is associated with altered song amplitude compared to undirected song.
source: In particular, female-directed song during courtship is associated with greater pitch and tempo, altered song amplitude, and increased acoustic stereotypy compared to the undirected song that male birds sing in isolation (Cooper and Goller, 2006; James and Sakata, 2015; Kao et al., 2005; Sakata et al., 2008; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980; Suri and Rajan, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Female-directed song during courtship is associated with increased acoustic stereotypy compared to undirected song.
source: In particular, female-directed song during courtship is associated with greater pitch and tempo, altered song amplitude, and increased acoustic stereotypy compared to the undirected song that male birds sing in isolation (Cooper and Goller, 2006; James and Sakata, 2015; Kao et al., 2005; Sakata et al., 2008; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980; Suri and Rajan, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pre-song heart rate is faster for directed song than undirected song.
source: Consistent with the notion that directed song reflects a state of greater physiological arousal, pre-song heart rate is faster for directed song than undirected song (Cooper and Goller, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: HVC receives strong cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain.
source: Moreover, the cortical premotor song nucleus HVC, like mammalian motor cortex, receives strong cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain (Ryan and Arnold, 1981; Zuschratter and Scheich, 1990), and cholinergic manipulations can alter excitability of HVC neurons in vitro and modulate their responses to song playback in vivo in anesthetized birds (Shea and Margoliash, 2003; Shea et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholinergic manipulations can alter excitability of HVC neurons in vitro.
source: Moreover, the cortical premotor song nucleus HVC, like mammalian motor cortex, receives strong cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain (Ryan and Arnold, 1981; Zuschratter and Scheich, 1990), and cholinergic manipulations can alter excitability of HVC neurons in vitro and modulate their responses to song playback in vivo in anesthetized birds (Shea and Margoliash, 2003; Shea et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholinergic manipulations can modulate HVC neuron responses to song playback in vivo in anesthetized birds.
source: Moreover, the cortical premotor song nucleus HVC, like mammalian motor cortex, receives strong cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain (Ryan and Arnold, 1981; Zuschratter and Scheich, 1990), and cholinergic manipulations can alter excitability of HVC neurons in vitro and modulate their responses to song playback in vivo in anesthetized birds (Shea and Margoliash, 2003; Shea et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Carbachol did not cause gross distortions of individual acoustic elements of song.
source: Carbachol did not cause gross distortions of the individual acoustic elements of the song, referred to as 'syllables' (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of spectrograms in Figure 1B showing preserved syllable structure.

claim: Carbachol effects on song paralleled those observed during female-directed song.
source: However, quantitative analysis revealed that carbachol had a number of consistent effects on syllable structure that largely paralleled those observed during female-directed song, including increases in pitch, syllable stereotypy, tempo, and amplitude (Cooper and Goller, 2006; James and Sakata, 2015; Kao et al., 2005; Sakata et al., 2008; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980; Suri and Rajan, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing carbachol effects to previously reported effects of social context, supported by citations.

claim: The effects produced by carbachol on pitch, pitch c.v., amplitude, and tempo were attenuated by the muscarinic antagonist atropine.
source: The effects produced by carbachol on pitch, pitch c.v., amplitude, and tempo were attenuated by the muscarinic antagonist atropine, but not by the nicotinic antagonists MEC (mecamylamine) and MLA (methyllycaconitine; Figures 1D, E, G and I; carbachol+atropine vs. carbachol+MEC+MLA, p<0.05 for all features except for tempo, signed-rank test; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects of muscarinic vs nicotinic antagonists (Figures 1D, E, G, I).

claim: The effects produced by carbachol on pitch, pitch c.v., amplitude, and tempo were not attenuated by the nicotinic antagonists MEC and MLA.
source: The effects produced by carbachol on pitch, pitch c.v., amplitude, and tempo were attenuated by the muscarinic antagonist atropine, but not by the nicotinic antagonists MEC (mecamylamine) and MLA (methyllycaconitine; Figures 1D, E, G and I; carbachol+atropine vs. carbachol+MEC+MLA, p<0.05 for all features except for tempo, signed-rank test; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects of muscarinic vs nicotinic antagonists (Figures 1D, E, G, I).

claim: Activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in HVC enhances song vigor.
source: In summary, we found that activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in HVC enhances song vigor, producing a suite of behavioral changes that largely parallels those observed during directed song (Cooper and Goller, 2006; James and Sakata, 2015; Kao et al., 2005; Sakata et al., 2008; Sossinka and Böhner, 1980; Suri and Rajan, 2018).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings with carbachol and antagonists.

claim: Carbachol significantly altered transition probabilities at variable transitions in song.
source: Consistent with the changes to sequencing observed during directed song, carbachol significantly altered transition probabilities at variable transitions in song ('branch points') (Figure 2A−C; n = 15 branch points, seven birds), and significantly increased the number of times that syllables were repeated (Figure 2D and E; carbachol vs. baseline, p=0.031, signed-rank test, n = 7 repeated syllables, six birds; Hampton et al., 2009; Sakata et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing changes in transition probabilities (Figure 2A-C).

claim: Carbachol significantly increased the number of times that syllables were repeated.
source: Consistent with the changes to sequencing observed during directed song, carbachol significantly altered transition probabilities at variable transitions in song ('branch points') (Figure 2A−C; n = 15 branch points, seven birds), and significantly increased the number of times that syllables were repeated (Figure 2D and E; carbachol vs. baseline, p=0.031, signed-rank test, n = 7 repeated syllables, six birds; Hampton et al., 2009; Sakata et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased repeat counts (Figure 2D, E).

claim: The effect of carbachol on syllable repetitions was greater for more variable repetitions.
source: Further, the effect on syllable repetitions was greater for more variable repetitions, as previously observed for temperature manipulations of HVC (Figure 2F; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between repeat length c.v. and normalized repeat count (Figure 2F, p=0.0012).

claim: LMAN is the main output nucleus of the AFP.
source: LMAN is the main output nucleus of the AFP, and muscimol inactivation of LMAN disconnects the AFP from the song motor pathway (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Ölveczky et al., 2011; Stepanek and Doupe, 2010; Warren et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Muscimol inactivation of LMAN disconnects the AFP from the song motor pathway.
source: LMAN is the main output nucleus of the AFP, and muscimol inactivation of LMAN disconnects the AFP from the song motor pathway (Andalman and Fee, 2009; Ölveczky et al., 2011; Stepanek and Doupe, 2010; Warren et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Infusion of muscimol caused a significant decrease in pitch variability, confirming that LMAN was effectively inactivated.
source: As in previous studies, infusion of muscimol caused a significant decrease in pitch variability, confirming that LMAN was effectively inactivated (reduction in pitch c.v.: 23 ± 5.3%, mean ± s.e.m.; muscimol vs. baseline, p=0.0020, signed-rank test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced pitch c.v. after muscimol infusion.

claim: Even when LMAN was inactivated, infusion of carbachol into HVC caused increases in pitch, pitch stereotypy, tempo, and amplitude.
source: However, even when LMAN was inactivated, infusion of carbachol into HVC caused increases in pitch, pitch stereotypy, tempo, and amplitude (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing carbachol effects persist during LMAN inactivation (Figure 3B-F).

claim: The changes elicited by combined carbachol + LMAN inactivation were not significantly different from the sum of the individual effects of carbachol and LMAN inactivation.
source: Moreover, for each feature, the changes elicited by combined carbachol + LMAN inactivation were not significantly different from the sum of the individual effects of carbachol and LMAN inactivation (pitch: p=0.77, pitch c.v.: p=0.85, tempo: p=0.22, amplitude: p=0.71, signed-rank test; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing additive effects of carbachol and LMAN inactivation.

claim: Increased cholinergic tone in HVC can modulate song via primary motor circuitry independently of input from the songbird basal ganglia.
source: These results indicate that increased cholinergic tone in HVC can modulate song via primary motor circuitry independently of input from the songbird basal ganglia, and thus provide support for a recent model proposing that basal ganglia and non-basal ganglia pathways can make independent and additive contributions to behavior (Yttri and Dudman, 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing carbachol effects persist during LMAN inactivation.

claim: Multi-unit activity in HVC is likely to primarily reflect interneuron activity.
source: Moreover, due to the higher firing rates of inhibitory interneurons relative to the excitatory projection neurons in HVC, such multi-unit activity is likely to primarily reflect interneuron activity (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Liberti et al., 2016; Rauske et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on known firing rate differences between cell types, supported by citations.

claim: During control saline blocks, there was no change in average firing rates relative to baseline.
source: During control saline blocks, there was no change in average firing rates relative to baseline, indicating that multiunit recordings remained stable over the period of drug dialysis (Figure 4C; change in firing rate in 100 ms window centered on syllable onsets: 1.1 ± 1.8%, mean ± s.e.m.; saline vs. baseline, p=0.64, signed-rank test; n = 118 multi-unit sites x syllables, five birds).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant change in firing rate during saline infusion (Figure 4C).

claim: Carbachol significantly increased average firing rates in HVC relative to baseline.
source: In contrast, we found that carbachol significantly increased average firing rates in HVC relative to baseline (Figure 4D; increase in firing rate in 100 ms window centered on syllable onsets: 9.9 ± 1.4%, mean ± s.e.m.; carbachol vs. baseline, p=2.8e-9, signed-rank test; n = 202 multi-unit sites x syllables, five birds; see also Figure 4—source data 1 for mixed effects analysis).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased firing rate during carbachol infusion (Figure 4D).

claim: On average there was a significant increase in firing rate both preceding and following syllable onsets after carbachol.
source: However, on average there was a significant increase in firing rate both preceding and following syllable onsets, with a modestly greater effect in the premotor window preceding syllable onsets (Figure 4D and E; maximum of 16% increase in firing rate at 25 ms before syllable onsets, minimum of 6.1% at 15 ms after syllable onsets).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing time-varying increases in firing rate (Figure 4D, E).

claim: On average, carbachol did not produce a significant change in Fano factor.
source: On average, carbachol did not produce a significant change in Fano factor (carbachol vs. saline, p>0.05 in 30 ms window preceding syllable onsets and 30 ms window after syllable onsets, rank-sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant change in Fano factor (Figure 4F).

claim: The increased pitch stereotypy caused by carbachol cannot be explained by reduced neural variability in HVC at the multi-unit level.
source: Thus, the increased pitch stereotypy caused by carbachol cannot be explained by reduced neural variability in HVC at the multi-unit level, though we cannot rule out the possibility that this increased behavioral stereotypy arises in part from reduced variability specifically among HVC projection neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Fano factor and spike count variance analyses.

claim: Previous studies have found only limited evidence that activity within HVC differs between undirected and directed song.
source: Directed song and microdialysis of carbachol into HVC were associated with similar behavioral changes, yet previous studies have found only limited evidence that activity within HVC differs between undirected and directed song (Jarvis et al., 1998; Matheson et al., 2016; Woolley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pattern of neural modulation with respect to song features was largely conserved across social contexts.
source: The pattern of neural modulation with respect to song features was largely conserved across social contexts: the mean ± s.e.m. correlation coefficient between directed and undirected firing rates was 0.90 ± 0.010 (e.g. Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; n = 151 multi-unit sites x syllables, 15 unique multi-unit sites, five birds).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing high correlation between directed and undirected firing rates.

claim: HVC multi-unit firing rates were consistently higher during directed song relative to undirected song.
source: Nevertheless, HVC multi-unit firing rates were consistently higher during directed song relative to undirected song (Figure 5B−5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; increase in firing rate in 100 ms window centered on syllable onsets: 7.2 ± 1.0%, mean ± s.e.m.; directed vs. undirected, p=1.1e-15, signed-rank test; n = 151 multi-unit sites x syllables, five birds; see also Figure 5—source data 1 for mixed effects analysis).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased firing rate during directed song (Figure 5B-D).

claim: The percent increase in firing rate for directed song was not significantly different from that observed after microdialysis of carbachol.
source: Further, the percent increase in firing rate for directed song was not significantly different from that observed after microdialysis of carbachol (p=0.90, rank-sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing firing rate increases between directed song and carbachol conditions.

claim: Blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in HVC with atropine caused an attenuation of social modulation for pitch and pitch c.v.
source: We found that blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in HVC with atropine caused an attenuation of social modulation for each of these features, which achieved significance for pitch and pitch c.v., but not song tempo (Figure 6C–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1; see also Figure 6—source data 1 for mixed effects analysis).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing atropine attenuated social modulation of pitch (p=0.046) and pitch c.v. (p=0.0028) (Figure 6D, E).

claim: Atropine caused a significant decrease in pitch and increase in pitch c.v. for directed song but had no effect on these features for undirected song.
source: We found that atropine caused a significant decrease in pitch and increase in pitch c.v. for directed song (relative to saline conditions), but had no effect on these features for undirected song (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects of atropine on directed vs undirected song (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: Increased cholinergic signaling in HVC normally contributes to the increased pitch and reduced pitch variability of directed song.
source: Thus, atropine attenuated a process that is specifically engaged during directed song, indicating that increased cholinergic signaling in HVC normally contributes to the increased pitch and reduced pitch variability of directed song.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the atropine experiments showing selective effects on directed song.

claim: The neural control of motor vigor is more distributed than has typically been recognized.
source: Our demonstration that cholinergic invigoration of song does not require participation of basal ganglia circuitry indicates that the neural control of motor vigor is more distributed than has typically been recognized.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing carbachol effects persist without basal ganglia.

claim: Prior experimental work and theoretical treatments of motor vigor have primarily focused on basal ganglia circuitry.
source: Prior experimental work and theoretical treatments of motor vigor have primarily focused on basal ganglia circuitry (Manohar et al., 2015; Panigrahi et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2008; Shadmehr et al., 2019; Yttri and Dudman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Basal ganglia circuits have been linked to shaping the vigor of motor output in the motivational context of goal-directed behaviors.
source: In particular, basal ganglia circuits have been linked to shaping the vigor of motor output in the motivational context of goal-directed behaviors—e.g. movements that are generated to obtain reward, with local dopaminergic signaling playing a key role (Berke, 2018; Dudman and Krakauer, 2016; Mazzoni et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2008; Turner and Desmurget, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholinergic modulation of forebrain motor circuitry may especially contribute to invigoration of behaviors that are adaptive in externally-triggered states of heightened physiological arousal.
source: In turn, cholinergic modulation of forebrain motor circuitry may especially contribute to invigoration of behaviors that are adaptive in externally-triggered states of heightened physiological arousal, like those that involve escape from danger, prey capture or courtship.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: RA serves as an intermediary between HVC and brainstem motor regions.
source: In the song system, the cortical motor nucleus RA serves as an intermediary between HVC and brainstem motor regions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about song system anatomy, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Cholinergic invigoration of song can be attributed to altered neural activity within the pathway from HVC→RA→brainstem.
source: Our findings indicate that cholinergic invigoration of song can be attributed to altered neural activity within this pathway (from HVC→RA→brainstem).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing carbachol effects persist without basal ganglia.

claim: Increased activity of RA projection neurons has been linked to increased pitch and amplitude via an excitatory influence on the relevant syringeal and respiratory muscles.
source: Such invigoration likely includes increased activity of RA projection neurons, which has been linked to increased pitch and amplitude via an excitatory influence on the relevant syringeal and respiratory muscles of the vocal apparatus (Goller and Riede, 2013; Sober et al., 2008; Srivastava et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacological excitation of RA projection neurons produces similar behavioral changes to microdialysis of carbachol into HVC.
source: Consistent with this model, pharmacological excitation of RA projection neurons (via manipulation of inhibition) produces similar behavioral changes to microdialysis of carbachol into HVC (Miller et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Multi-unit recordings in HVC are thought to primarily sample from the inhibitory interneurons.
source: Multi-unit recordings in HVC are thought to primarily sample from the inhibitory interneurons, due to the fact that this population is considerably more active than the projection neurons during song and awake quiescent periods (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Liberti et al., 2016; Rauske et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on known firing rate differences, supported by citations.

claim: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor agonists depolarize both classes of projection neurons and hyperpolarize interneurons in HVC.
source: However, a model in which acetylcholine suppresses HVC projection neuron activity during song is difficult to reconcile with the cellular effects of acetylcholine measured in acute slice electrophysiology experiments: muscarinic acetylcholine receptor agonists depolarize both classes of projections neurons and hyperpolarize interneurons (Shea et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Injections of carbachol into HVC of anesthetized songbirds increase spontaneous activity within RA.
source: Notably, injections of carbachol into HVC of anesthetized songbirds increase spontaneous activity within RA (Shea and Margoliash, 2003), supporting the view that acetylcholine increases the activity of the HVCRA neurons in particular.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Acetylcholine increases the activity of all major cell classes within HVC in tandem.
source: In sum, our data and prior literature suggest a model in which acetylcholine increases the activity of all major cell classes within HVC in tandem.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on integration of current findings with prior literature.

claim: A coordinated increase in activity among the major excitatory and inhibitory cell classes within HVC occurs normally during the transition from non-singing quiescent periods to active song production.
source: Such a coordinated increase in activity among the major excitatory and inhibitory cell classes within HVC also occurs normally during the transition from non-singing quiescent periods to active song production (Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007), and is broadly consistent with the tight coupling of excitation and inhibition that has been observed in mammalian cortical regions (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Haider et al., 2006; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Wehr and Zador, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most previous studies that have manipulated HVC activity have not reported a reduction in behavioral variability.
source: Most previous studies that have manipulated HVC activity have not reported a reduction in behavioral variability (Hamaguchi et al., 2016; Long and Fee, 2008; Zhang et al., 2017; but see Isola et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lesions and pharmacological inactivation of the AFP output nucleus LMAN reduce pitch variability substantially.
source: In contrast, lesions and pharmacological inactivation of the AFP output nucleus LMAN reduce pitch variability substantially (Hampton et al., 2009; Kao and Brainard, 2006; Kao et al., 2005; Stepanek and Doupe, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HVC projection neurons exhibit extremely low trial-to-trial variability.
source: The observation that HVC projection neurons exhibit extremely low trial-to-trial variability also might suggest that HVC does not introduce substantial behavioral variability (Hahnloser et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A significant source of behavioral variability originates within HVC.
source: In contrast, our findings suggest that a significant source of behavioral variability originates within HVC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing carbachol reduces pitch variability.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease or basal ganglia damage engage in fewer volitional movements and exhibit a reduced willingness to exert effort to obtain reward.
source: Patients with Parkinson's disease or basal ganglia damage engage in fewer volitional movements and exhibit a reduced willingness to exert effort to obtain reward, suggesting that reduced motor vigor in these patients is primarily motivational in nature (Mazzoni et al., 2007; Schmidt et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parkinson's disease patients can exhibit 'paradoxical' movements in situations that provoke extreme emotion.
source: However, these patients can exhibit 'paradoxical' movements in situations that provoke extreme emotion (Bonanni et al., 2010; Glickstein and Stein, 1991), and can effectively modulate grip strength when explicitly instructed to do so, even while exhibiting deficits in the modulation of grip strength by reward (Schmidt et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parkinson's patients can exhibit improvements in movement vigor in response to engaging sensory stimulation.
source: Similarly, Parkinson's patients can exhibit improvements in movement vigor in response to engaging sensory stimulation (McIntosh et al., 1997; Rubinstein et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arousal-dependent motor invigoration in Parkinson's patients could be enabled by cholinergic modulation of cortical motor circuitry.
source: Our results indicate that such arousal-dependent motor invigoration in these patients could be enabled by cholinergic modulation of cortical motor circuitry.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Alzheimer's disease is principally associated with the loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain and diminished cholinergic innervation of the cortex.
source: Particularly noteworthy in this respect is the slowing of gait, reduced force generation, and loss of verbal fluency that are frequently observed in patients with Alzheimer's disease (Buchman et al., 2007; Ferris and Farlow, 2013; Goldman et al., 1999), which is principally associated with the loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain and diminished cholinergic innervation of the cortex (Francis et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of movement vigor may precede, and be predictive of, subsequent cognitive decline in Alzheimer's and other diseases.
source: Indeed, loss of movement vigor may precede, and be predictive of, subsequent cognitive decline in Alzheimer's and other diseases (Buchman et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous neural recordings from HVCX projection neurons in zebra finches did not reveal conspicuous differences between social contexts.
source: While previous neural recordings from HVCX projection neurons in zebra finches did not reveal conspicuous differences between social contexts (Woolley et al., 2014), the other cell classes in HVC were not examined, as was implicitly done here by recording multi-unit activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: One study of the expression of the immediate early gene EGR-1 in HVC of Bengalese finches reported differences between social contexts.
source: However, consistent with our findings, one study of the expression of the immediate early gene (IEG) EGR-1 in HVC of Bengalese finches reported differences between social contexts (Matheson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous work has identified dopaminergic and noradrenergic signaling within song system nuclei as contributing to social modulation of song.
source: The contribution of the cholinergic system to the social modulation of song is also noteworthy, given that previous work has identified dopaminergic and noradrenergic signaling within song system nuclei as contributing to social modulation of song (Castelino and Ball, 2005; Glaze, 2017; Ihle et al., 2015; Leblois et al., 2010; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arousal levels vary over slower timescales in relation to circadian rhythms.
source: Beyond the rapid changes in arousal elicited by changes in social context, arousal levels also vary over slower timescales in relation to circadian rhythms, and this variation in arousal may contribute to circadian changes in song and neural activity in song control regions (Chi and Margoliash, 2001; Day et al., 2009; Derégnaucourt et al., 2005; Glaze and Troyer, 2006; Liberti et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Female birds are attentive to the differences between undirected and female-directed song, and they prefer the latter.
source: Indeed, behavioral studies have demonstrated that female birds are attentive to the differences between undirected and female-directed song, and that they prefer the latter (Dunning et al., 2014; Woolley and Doupe, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The quality of song in some bird species differs between affiliative interactions in a courtship setting versus territorial interactions between males, or interactions with juveniles.
source: For example, the quality of song in some bird species differs between affiliative interactions in a courtship setting versus territorial interactions between males, or interactions with juveniles (Chen et al., 2016; Trillo and Vehrencamp, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Features such as loudness, pitch, and tempo of human speech can be decoded to make inferences about the affective state of the speaker.
source: This parallels the observation for human speech that features such as loudness, pitch, and tempo can be decoded to make inferences about the affective state of the speaker (Banse and Scherer, 1996; Fairbanks and Pronovost, 1938; Leinonen et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.
